newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-'Blood & Oil' - Potent mix in book on Iran.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-'Blood & Oil' - Potent mix in book on Iran.

text.p: From a feudal society to the shah's ostentatious stabs at modernity to the Islamic fundamentalism of the ayatollahs, oil has been central to Iran's dramatic 20th century transitions.

In "Blood & Oil, Memoirs of a Persian Prince," Manucher Farmanfarmaian tells the fascinating tale from first-hand knowledge. Born to wealth and privilege in 1917 -- his ancestors ruled Persia before the Pahlavi shahs -- he became a mover and shaker in Iran's oil industry.

But after the Iranian revolution, he escaped with little more than a gold watch and his memories. Now a citizen of Venezuela, where he owns a potato chip factory, Farmanfarmaian told Reuters in an interview in Washington that his story could be told only in the United States, and he hopes the telling may help to clear away some misunderstandings.

His Princeton-educated daughter, Roxanne, a Middle East specialist who published a magazine in pre-revolutionary Iran, helped him write his memoirs, moving to Venezuela and working at his side for almost five years. She now works in San Francisco as West Coast editor of Publishers Weekly.

Both feel that Americans need to understand Iran to avoid further missteps in that vital area of the Middle East, where the oil-rich country, despite U.S. sanctions, maintains trade with about 100 countries and, unlike its neighbours, has been politically stable since the 1979 Islamic revolution.
BOTH A BLESSING AND A CURSE
Oil blessed and cursed Iran, the Farmanfarmaians say. Oil brought immense wealth but it was largely controlled by the British, who developed the oil industry and treated Iran as "a virtual colony."

Americans "think that the British were angels," Farmanfarmaian said. He thinks differently. "They were exactly the same people who fought a war with the Americans in Boston. They were not changed, their system of colonialism had not changed ... they were successful, why should they change?"

"People complain," he said, "why didn't we take strong steps to get our rights? We couldn't, the British were all-powerful -- in the whole of the Middle East. Every time the government attempted something strong before 1951, before nationalisation (of the oil industry), the British would come to say, we will topple the government, they will abolish everything there -- so we couldn't do it."

Although Farmanfarmaian studied petroleum engineering at Birmingham University in England, he chose not to work for the British-controlled Anglo-Iranian oil company on his return; he felt he would be treated like the Persian servants of British friends --"decked out in sumptuous uniform but with naked feet -- a potent reminder of their servile position."
Eventually he became the shah's oil adviser and, despite the shah's disapproval, he was instrumental in creating the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

After Mohammed Mossadeq, his cousin, nationalised the oil industry, the United States and its "Seven Sisters" oil companies took over as the dominant foreign power in Iran. But after a U.S.-directed coup overthrew Mossadeq in 1953, the Iranian people turned against the United States.
"The Americans, who themselves had advocated democracy, unfortunately took the blame for abolishing democracy," Farmanfarmaian said.
LAND REFORM A MISTAKE

"Blood & Oil" argues that American pressure on Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi to take land from rich landowners -- Farmanfarmaian and his large family among them -- and give it to the peasants was bad policy for Iran at that stage.

Land reform alienated the people, Farmanfarmanian said, because the peasants who got the land had to pay taxes and maintenance to the shah, and they had no money with which to do so. "Land ownership was destroyed, but it was not replaced by anything else," he said. Illiterate peasants moved to the cities, but there they found no housing and no jobs.

"People thought they could make themselves rich with oil money, but what country did it? Are Algeria, Kuwait, Iraq, Venezuela developed? This is just a chimeric idea that in five years' time, because you have money, you can develop a modern country," Farmanfarmaian said.

He criticises British greed and short-sighted American geopolitical expediency but he also blames the shah for palace intrigues and paranoia, grand dreams and empty promises. And he blames himself and other aristocratic Iranians.

"Our European educations went only skin deep," he wrote in a prologue to his story. "We did not bring discipline or order to our country. We allowed ourselves to live surrounded by ignorance. We were decadent, like the lords of the ancien regime. But instead of Napoleon we got Khomeini."

His daughter is hopeful the landslide election of moderate Mohammad Khatami as president in May can spark a change in U.S. policy toward Iran, where "about half the population is under 25 -- they don't even remember the shah. They want to westernize and they're pushing the clerical regime."

If U.S. policy of extending MFN to China is intended to further human rights, she asked, why not follow a similar policy toward Iran? "The more Barbie dolls that are there, the more likely that terrorism will not be exported."
